utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good afternoon to everyone. May we have the appearances for today, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Joanna Korner, Matthew Olmsted, and Crispian Smith for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, Eugene O'Sullivan, and Ms. Tatjana Savic appearing for Stanisic Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Igor Pantelic and Dragan Krgovic for Zupljanin Defence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I just would like to ask the permission of the Trial Chamber to be excused because I have the interview with the OTP witness scheduled at 2.30. So I will be leaving for 45 minutes. Thank you very much. Please, Ms. Korner. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, Your Honours, the ruling on that motion has not been made. But the Prosecution, if Your Honours think it's right and -- and think that the Defence have -- have a point, have no objection to re-calling ST-179. And it may be that the simplest thing, subject to us being able to get a hold of him and being able to making arrangements, is that that is the time when he's re-called. It won't take up the two days that's been set aside, but it's at least something. Failing that, we could attempt to get hold of ST-142. He is quite a big witness as far as the Stanisic team are concerned, but it would -- we'd be giving them, effectively, if we can get hold of him, four days' notice. He's, again, a -- I think he's a -- he is a 92 ter witness. But, Your Honours, if -- I think what we'd need today, if that's possible, simply a decision on that part of the Defence's application, namely, that we should re-call for further cross-examination ST-179. Your Honours, the Defence set out their position in -- in their application. As I say, we have no objection, if Your Honours think that the application has merit. So that's the first matter. I don't know whether Your Honours want to consider that now or perhaps consider it over the -- after the -- during the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Do Defence counsel on either side have a -- any observations to make on this matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, it would be -- it would be preferable for the Defence of Stanisic that the first solution is adopted, which is the re-calling of ST-179. We stated our reasons for -- for our request to re-call that witness based on the disclosure of the -- of the witness which have been delayed disclosure which is the witness which was supposed to appear next week. Therefore, we would -- we gave our reasons in -- in a written form, and I wouldn't like to repeat them once again in the -- in the open court. The -- as for the other solution, the calling of the other witness, we feel that we ask and explained to Ms. Korner that we would need at least seven to eight days to prepare for that witness, so we -- we asked them to notify us about his coming a bit in advance than usual. So in that respect, we would also welcome a decision of the Trial Chamber in the course of today's sitting. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... that's the first matter. Then, Your Honours, Your Honours may think this is good news, particularly in the light of our still pending application to add the witnesses to deal with adjudicated facts. We are not going to be calling the witness with the number ST-206. That's a very lengthy witness. We had him down, I think, for eight hours. And we've taken the decision not to call him. The Defence have been notified of that last week. And we did notify Your Honours; we're not sure that we -- that you took in - I don't mean it that way - because we didn't have any response to it. We're not calling, either, ST-119. So, as I say, we are -- you'll remember, when Your Honours were telling us to reduce our witness list early on, I said it was almost certain that we would be reducing it by a natural attrition, and so we are. So that's actually removed quite a number of hours from the witness list. Your Honours, we then have the question of Ewa Tabeau. We filed an application on the 10th of March, applying to add her report, "Victims of War," to her earlier report. And we haven't -- the -- on the 24th of March, the Defence opposed that and since then we haven't heard anything at all, nor am I sure that we've had a ruling that she's to be treated as an expert. We wish to call her at the end of July, just before the break, we're having some difficulty in filling -- finding witnesses. We appreciate that the Defence may not want to cross-examine until after the break, particularly as we haven't had a ruling yet one way or another on the second report, and so we were going to suggest that she is called; she'd be the last witness on the Wednesday -- no, Thursday, working on the basis that her report would go in, and we'd ask for a couple of hours or so extra with her on the Thursday before the break and then be cross-examined after the break. But we do need rulings. And, Your Honours, I think, as far as I'm aware, unless I get an e-mail to the contrary from anybody, that those were the matters that I wanted to raise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So noted, Ms. Korner. Before the scheduled witness is brought in, are there any other preliminary matters that need engage the Chamber's attention?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Can you hear me, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Please make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, sir, and thank you for coming to assist the Tribunal in its work. The first thing that I would do is to remind you that the solemn declaration that you have just made would expose you to the pain of the penalty of perjury should you give false or mislead testimony to this Tribunal. The first formal questions that the Chamber has of you is to ask to you state your name, your date of birth, and your ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Lazar. My last name is Drasko. I was born on 15th of January, 1948, in Tasovcici, municipality of Capljina, in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And what is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm a Serb by ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And would you tell us what your profession is, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Currently, I'm -- I work as a prosecutor at the cantonal prosecutor's office in Gorazde, Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: You said "currently." Were you doing something differently before that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly. I graduated from law school in 1970, in Sarajevo. After that, I was an intern at the district court in Mostar until 1973 at -- when I passed my bar exam. In that year, I was elected judge for the municipal court in Capljina. I was a judge at that court, and I spent a year with the JNA at Bileca, Pancevo, and Skopje. And later, I continued. And I believe it was in 1976 that I was elected prosecutor at the municipal prosecutor's office in Capljina, which covers the municipalities of Stolac, Ljubinje, and Neum. In that position I remained until about 1983. Then I became deputy director of the health centre in Capljina where I stayed for four years. That was after the infamous Neum scandal when I had to leave. And in 1988, after that scandal, the Assembly of the Republic started electing people for those positions. And I opened a private attorney's office in Capljina, where I worked until the beginning of the war, I believe until the 1st of May, when I was drafted. I was drafted to the VRS in Tasovcici, my -- the place where I was born.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Have you testified previously before this Tribunal or before any -- courts in any of the countries in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The procedure of this Tribunal is such as would not be unfamiliar to you in that the -- you have been called by one side - in this case, the Prosecution - and the counsel for each of the accused would have a right to cross-examine you. In terms of the time, the Prosecution has been granted a total of two-hours to conduct their examination-in-chief. And counsel for the accused Stanisic, two hours; and counsel for the accused Zupljanin, an additional hour. The -- the Bench, after any re-examination the Prosecution may have, would themselves have any questions -- may themselves have questions of you; and, after that, your testimony would be -- would be at an end. Ordinarily, the sittings of the Tribunal would be in this case an afternoon sitting; we would sit until 7.00 in the evening. And there are two 20 minute breaks in between that. The sittings do not exceed an hour and a half for technical reasons having to do with the taping system where tapes have to be changed. But if, before the ordinary time of a break, you are in distress or for any reason you need a break, you could indicate that to the Chamber, and we would, of course, accommodate you. With that, I would invite counsel for the Prosecution to begin the examination-in-chief. Yes, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Drasko.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you. You've already provided a part of your professional background. I wanted to start where you left off. You said in May you were mobilised into the army in Tasovcici. In early June, 1992, were you relocated to Bileca?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: Yes. There was an offensive against Tasovcici and the entire Neretva valley, and we Serbs, as well as those who were with us, who failed to be Yugoslavs, Croats and Muslims alike, withdrew toward Nevesinje. That's what my sister did. And I went to Bileca with my children. The offensive went on for a few days. There wasn't fighting -- there was no fighting, there were no casualties. Only later I knew that -- I found out that it was pursuant to the Boban-Karadzic Agreement. So the Croatian troops did not cut us off at Stolac, but, rather, we were able to get out safely.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What was your position that you held when you were in Bileca?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: First, my position was that of an invalid. I had broken a leg and had to an infirmary where I was treated, and I spent 15 days there in a stationary unit. So when the fracture had healed, I was called up by Slobodan Cup [phoen] from Mostar; he is a lawyer by trade, and in the army he was a reserve officer. And he invited me to join them in the command of the corps because I had graduated from the reserve officers school in Bileca. I was a reserve officer. Apart from that, I attended the police school at Pancevo, and later on I was at Skoplje, too. So I had completed a course for military police commander. After leaving the army, I was Deputy Commander of the staff -- army staff for Herzegovina. Divjak worked there, too. And our last commander was a Macedonian. I visited him and I saw that Yugoslavia was breaking up, and I saw that genocide was under way and I asked him to do something so as to prevent the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. Mr. Drasko, I know you really want to provide a lot of information, but please try to focus on the questions that I'm asking. When you went to Bileca, I understand you were in hospital for --

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: -- a bit. Then you stated that you'd joined the corps there. Would that be the Herzegovina Corps?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: Yes, the Herzegovina Corps. The security service which was commanded by Captain Segrt. I served under him and worked on administrative tasks and legal affairs. There were also cases when perpetrators of some criminal offences had to be examined, especially perpetrators of murder. The problem was that the offences were committed by military personnel, but military courts were not functioning. And we would transfer such cases to the district prosecutor's office in Trebinje.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And how long did you remain in this position with the Herzegovina Corps?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: About a month and a half. There were two small children with me, and my wife remained behind as a prisoner at the Dretelj camp, and my children slept with me, so they understood it was better for me to go home and take care of the children. And also Colonel Nikola Milosevic didn't like my saying that there was such a thing as the Dretelj camp and that neither the army nor the international community were doing anything for my friends and other people to be released from that camp. He -- his position was that I was a panic-maker. So he said, Go home. My wife was exchanged and was able to leave the camp on the 18th of August. I had already been at home with my children for some 15 days. When I say "at home," I say in an apartment that was given to some friends of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, next, after you left Bileca, you held two positions simultaneously in Visegrad. What were those positions?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: I arrived in Bileca on the 28th of August. We found some temporary accommodation. And, after that, I reported to the corps command. I was first drafted in by the army, where I was in charge of the legal affairs. But I was also told that there were crimes and that they don't have a prosecutor, and I was immediately offered to be elected to the civilian prosecutor at the district court and that I should take up that duty because there were murders going on and its an urgent matter. And then I went to the court, the Judge Milanka Tanaskovic gave me the files, she gave me the keys. I saw the files, and then I drafted the requests for investigation. But then, after completing that, every day I would return to the corps command where we also performed guard duty during night. Occasionally, we were there for communication purposes. We drafted criminal reports and did other legal jobs.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: The record states that you were a prosecutor for the district court. Just to clarify, were you a basic public prosecutor in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: Basic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And when did you first begin performing the function of basic prosecutor? When did you start actually taking in case files?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: The republic Assembly of Republika Srpska appointed me, I think, on the 31st of October to this position, and since that day, I was able to conduct these tasks. But there were other cases that I had done prior to that date. I spent most of my time in TG Rudo until the 31st of January next year.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... and I understand that you're --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sorry, I didn't mean to interrupt. I understand that you were formally appointed to the basic prosecutor's position on the 31st of October, 1992. But when did you actually start performing the role? I understand that you started performing it before that.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: Yes, I have mentioned that prior to my official appointment, and that was several days after my arrival in Visegrad, I was told that there were two or three murderers there who were in remand prison at the command and that requests should be drafted by me for investigation. I did draft them, and I then forwarded them to the court so that the investigation may start, so the cases would start being processed. They believed it was right thing to do because soon I were to be elected prosecutor where there was nobody holding that position at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, you were basic public prosecutor in Visegrad until 2001; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And after that you were district court judge in Trebinje until 2003; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: In the district court of Trebinje, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And then from there, in 2003, you were -- started working for the cantonal prosecutor's office in Gorazde. And that's where you've worked ever since; right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: In Gorazde, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, can you --

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct. However, I'm not the chief prosecutor since 2008. I am just a prosecutor, and Bilajica Miksa [phoen] is now the chief prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Right. Now, when you -- when you arrived in Bileca, who was commander of the Herzegovina Corps?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: I think it was Radomir, Radomir Grubac.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's take -- let's take a look at 65 ter 3080. And we can see that this is a report from the Herzegovina Corps command dated 4 June 1992. And if we could turn to the last page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, could you give us the tab number, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This is tab 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Drasko, if you could take a look at the signature. Is that the signature of Colonel Grubac?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: I think it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could look at page 2 of the B/C/S and page 3 of the English. And we look at item number 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: It states that Lieutenant-Colonel General Mladic and Radovan Karadzic attended the SAO Herzegovina Assembly held in Bileca. Mr. Drasko, do you recall that President Karadzic and General Mladic were in Bileca in early July 1992?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: At the time, I was in Tasovcici, in trenches. I wasn't informed about this. I wasn't working at the command at the time, only in my unit. In the Tasovcici area, where only me and my cousin were Serbs, all the rest of them were Muslims, we didn't have too much contact with the Herzegovina Corps, and we didn't get all that many information. But I did hear -- because what people were saying was when Radovan coming to Bileca, then territories fall. They were immediately afraid that the area of Herzegovina would fall into the their hands, after having heard that he has arrived. They were saying, God, please don't have them come over. Not even the fighters liked him coming over. They believed he was selling things out. The people found out about the agreement between him and Boban that was reached in Grac. Momo Mandic also spoke about that. And the rumour went that some parts of Herzegovina would be handed over in exchange for Posavina. People in that part of Herzegovina weren't really pleased with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Drasko. Let me remind you, please keep your answers short and try to focus on my question. There is a delay with the translations, and so just because there is a delay --

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Just because there is a delay doesn't mean that I'm waiting for you to finish your answer necessarily and to continue with it. Please keep your answers short. Well, I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May I tender this into evidence, Your Honours, this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's take --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I apologise. As Exhibit P1477, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And, for the record, it's not 3580 but 3080, 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, you're right, Your Honour. I apologise. Let's take a look at 65 ter 1460. We can see this is a report from the Herzegovina Corps command dated 11 June 1992. If we can turn to the last page of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And can you confirm for us again whether this is the signature of Colonel Grubac?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could now turn to page 2 of the B/C/S; page 5 of the English. We see here that it reports that a prisoner accommodation centre was holding 244 people, including 16 women and several minors. Where was this accommodation centre?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: The centre was located in an old building built by the Austrians, next to the Mose Pijade Museum where the command was and where the office were of Mr. Grubac. I was -- I had my offices at the ground floor, and that's where Commander Segrt was also located, and he was on the first floor. And in direction of Bileca, immediately next to us was this big building where the prisoners were located. These people were in terrible conditions. One could smell the sweat, the heavy stench of sweat. It was summertime, it was hot, they couldn't wash really often, and one could smell them passing by the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what was the ethnicity of these persons at this centre?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: I think that in the collection centre it was either Muslims or Croats. There were a few Serbs who were also there but because they were considered to be deserters or traitors. But there were very few of them. Mile Sakovski, for instance, was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: It states further --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we turn to page 3 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: It states --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And stay where we are for the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: It states: On 10 June, the organs of the Bileca SO and SUP carried out the illegal weapons seizure operation. Several people were arrested on that occasion, of whom 41 were accommodated in the barracks. Is that referring to the barracks next to the Mose Pijade Museum or -- what we were just talking about?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: I heard that police kept their detainees somewhere else, that they were not together with the other group. They were guarded by a different group of people. And I know that police released these people, let's them go to Montenegro, whether -- whereas the other group of prisoners were then exchanged in Stolac. I heard, while I was in Bileca, that there was an action or operation involving Muslims, armed Muslims, who surrounded the Serbian forces. The Serbian forces gave them their weapons, and then they took them to the town and put them into a prison. And then, later on, they were transported by buses to Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes. I want to focus on this particular document because it mentions that these 41 persons were accommodated in the barracks and mentions the barracks. And I just want to clarify: Would that be the Mose Pijade barracks?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: There was one barracks, Mose Pijade, but the police also had somewhere a prison of their own, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned, I think, an incident that you observed. In June 1992, did you see a group of non-Serbs in the custody of the police in Bileca?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you describe what -- can you describe what you saw?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: I've heard of that. I don't know exactly where, but I do know that the people who were forced to take off their clothes were taken to a barracks, most probably in Bileca, and that these people were later transported by buses to Montenegro. And they were held there for about a month or a month and a half. One of the girls who worked in the same barracks with me, she had a boyfriend, and he -- she went with -- with him to Montenegro, and I remember her bringing me chocolate later on and telling me that he will be released. And eventually these people arrived in Montenegro and then found their accommodation there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I want to clarify something for the record. Did you actually observe these non-Serbs who were in the custody of the police? Did you see it for yourself?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: I saw for myself when they were taken through town in a convoy. They passed through the old part of town, next to the mosque, old mosque that was far from the building of the -- where the command was located. I was with my children when I saw them. I don't know where, on what premises were they accommodated. I didn't manage to find that out. Actually, I wasn't all that much interested in that because these people were not prisoners of the Herzegovina Corps but the prisoners of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You said something about their clothing. What were they wearing when you saw them being escorted through the town?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: They had only their underwear. It was summertime, and they had only their underwear on.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May this be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1478, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: In early July, did you see any bus convoys for non-Serbs in Bileca?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: Commander Segrt told me to go towards the lake in direction of Niksica, outside of the garrison, and that I should go and see the buses there. He didn't explain what was I supposed to look at. But he was that kind of a person. He would never say anything like that. Specifically, he wanted, me to see for myself. He would never specifically tell me, Do such and such a thing, or make a categorical order. I think Captain Duka told me later that they had a fight. I saw some buses, but I didn't know where they were going, who these people. He didn't tell me anything. But I asked some people, and they told me they were Muslims being taken away. And then on my return, I told him I've seen some buses, people being taken away. And I asked him, So what am I supposed to do? And he said, Well, your job was to go and see what was going on, to determine the situation that. That was his answer. And then I realised that civilians were also being transported away from Bileca.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And from what you could tell, who organised this convoy of buses?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: I think it was organised by the authorities of Bileca and the police of the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's take a look at 65 ter 45.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What we have in front of us is a letter from SJB Gacko to the Herzegovina Corps dated 29 July 1992. You can see that the letter refers to the Bileca prison. Which detention facility is being referred to there?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: Detention centre was located in Bileca. Milan Soldo, who previously had worked in the Mostar prisoner, was in charge of that prison. He was the main person who was in charge there. They have -- didn't have enough food. And then Gruban [phoen] insisted that these people should be exchanged or released because we didn't have -- they didn't have food for them. And then Soldo made a list of the oldest people there; they were released. I was among those who were escorting them. They were taken to Stolac. There was no exchange. I didn't really appreciate that because my wife was at the time in Dretelj prison. She could have been exchanged, but Grubac decided not do that. But, of course, I was soldier, and I didn't complain. I was really displeased. I thought that they should allow people from Capljina also to get out, the civilians. But, in any case, people did get out. And then later on there was an exchange on the 28th of August when the others were released.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I just want to clarify. When it's referring in this letter to the Herzegovina Corps, to this Bileca prison, it's referring to someplace different than the Mose Pijade barracks. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: It is all one facility in a fortress, immediately in front of the command building. There is only a road between the two buildings. And the other side were the premises where we would bring the prisons in for examination, and on the first floor it was a cafe. And then further on there were accommodation with beds for us and the military police. That's where I slept with my three children as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, it says here that it's talking about Muslims who were detained at this facility. Can you tell us, Were these Muslim prisoners -- were they civilians or were they participating in the armed conflict?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: From what I knew, all these people were my neighbours, so to speak. I was a judge in Capljina and Stolac, and all these people were my neighbours who had been picked up by paramilitary formations before the fall of Capljina. For instance, Meho, a neighbour of mine who used to drink coffee with me every day, he was there at the command. Many prominent people from Mostar was also brought there, people I had known from before. I tried to have a word with them, but I also wanted to register them. They were looking for someone to help them be released, but then I -- we told them that the -- wait, there's going to be an exchange, be patient. And Soldo was in touch with the people. These people were -- also included farmers from Dubrave area. And when -- when they were being released, one of them told me, Don't worry, Lazar, we'll make sure that your wife gets released as well. Also, in Dubrave, there were people who used to fight together with us, on our side, with the Serbs, and yet they were also brought there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Just to clarify what you're telling us: These Muslims detained at this location, they were not participating in the armed conflicts; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: They were not. They even lived among the Serbs in Stolac, Domanovici, Capljina, Mostar, Pijesti [phoen], and so on and so forth. And with the withdrawal of Serbs, some of them were taken along. Some of them were driven from there. And also because Serbs wanted to have some people to use as hostages who they can later on exchange. Most probably that was another reason. I apologise, there were many prisoners, Serbs, Yugoslavs, who were held in Capljina, Grabovina, Dretelj, and private prisons. In Dretelj, there were, at the time, 2- or 300 prisons.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So why were these non-Serbs detained at the prison? Why were they being held there?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: To be honest, I think only because they were Serbs -- or, rather, because they were not Serbs. I knew these people; none of them were responsible for any sabotage activities or for having killed anyone. On several occasions, I sat together with Ekrem Codarevic in a hotel. UNPROFOR was also present, and we analysed the situation. And he told me, Be careful, Lazar, Radovan sold you out; don't stay here too long. Move to Bileca, outside of the borders of Banovina of Croatia, and that way you will survive. And later on I found about the agreement, so I realised that it actually happened, that there was agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This letter is to the attention of Colonel Milosevic. What role did Colonel Milosevic play in prisoner exchanges?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: Milosevic simply believed the Croat side when -- in their claims that the camp of Dretelj does not exist, that the exchange would be of the all-for-all type. He didn't like me saying that the Dretelj camp exists, that people are being tortured, women and so on. He believed I was making lies and propaganda. And at the time of the exchange, a colleague told me --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt. You misunderstood my question, though. I want to know what role Colonel Milosevic played in prisoner exchanges, because this letter from SJB Gacko is addressed to him. Was he at all responsible for prisoner exchanges?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: He was exclusively in charge of the exchanges of prisoners. He was a very serious man, and I believed he would accomplish a lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May this be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1479, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, before we let this document go, could we just inquire with the witness. Under whose command this prison in Bileca was? Because I thought I heard the witness say that it was run by the police; yet the request for exchange seems to have been made to the Colonel from the army. So who was responsible for running this camp; do you know? Or can we ask the witness about this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Prisoners who -- that were located in the corps command were prisoners of the army. And military units were in charge of them, primarily Milosevic and Grubac from the security service. They were making the plans for the release of these people; whereas the prisoners who were in town, they were under the police command, and it was the police who was making decisions about them. They released those towards Montenegro; and the corps released their prisoners to Dubrave, Capljina, Ljuboski, and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you able to say how many were detained in the civilian centre where the police was running it and how many detainees were held by the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot say precisely for the police. They're probably the numbers put forward by the Prosecutor. And as for the army, I believe that there were as many as 600 people kept by the military in these buildings, because they were full. Soldo told me that Grubac had ordered a separation of all elderly people and that they should all be released without an exchange at Stolac. And that was done. In cooperation with the Croatian authorities, they were let go to Stolac. And the younger ones were kept until the last exchange on the 18th, 18th of August; that was the day of the last exchange, and I was present there. It was interesting because they tricked Colonel Milosevic on that occasion. He was to -- he trusted them too much. It should have been an exchange all for all. There were two trucks full of young recruits from the JNA who should have been exchanged. When the civilians, especially HOS members, Kospic [phoen], Puntic [phoen], and others who I knew well, they were taken prisoner and they were HOS members from Dretelj. When they crossed the border-line, the exchange was stopped, and the young recruits were taken back and they killed them all. Only recently have their bodies -- were their bodies discovered in the surroundings of Vinodol. At least 80 soldiers were killed there. And if it had been a real exchange, if they had been careful enough, if Colonel Milosevic hadn't trusted the Croatian authorities as much, if he had been more distrustful, these people would now be alive. My wife was also released on that occasion; I was present. I pointed her out to Milosevic and said, She was also from Dretelj camp. There were about 80 women and over 120 men there. Do you trust me now? But he didn't say a word. And that was why he drove me out of the garrison. After that, he died soon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And just to clarify further what Judge Harhoff asked you: Where the police held non-Serbs, was this in the same compound as the Mose Pijade barracks, or was it off that site?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: It was in the barracks, in old buildings built by the Austrians, about 50 metres from the command of the security; whereas Grubac had his office on the upper floor. I served my compulsory army service there too, 1975. I know every metre of the premises.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I want to move on to Visegrad now. Can you tell us, I think you mentioned that you arrived in Visegrad at the end of August; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: On 28th of August with my wife when she was released from the camp and three small children aged 4 through 11. That's how we arrived at Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Before you arrived in Visegrad, do you recall hearing announcements over the radio coming from the Visegrad municipal authorities?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: My in-laws said to me that they had heard that. That they were inviting people to come there, that there were vacant houses, that houses would be distributed. But I first decided to go to Trebinje to see Dobroslav Cuk, the chief of the Red Cross, who is now president of Trebinje municipality. My wife brought a list of the remaining prisoners. She was a doctor, a microbiologist. But that was mostly due to the row I had with Ms. Hartman from the Red Cross delegation, and I blamed her for these people remaining in the camp. And in the end she had made a list of the remaining people in the camp, and we inquired whether there was a position of judge for me at Trebinje because I was much more experienced than the judges there and if my wife could get a job as a doctor there. But they refused. They were saying, No, there are no jobs for you there. And only then did we decide to go to Visegrad. I didn't come to Bileca on a white horse as a hero or a cadre of theirs, but I came as a refugee, with a refugee ID.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Drasko. But, please, please, focus on the questions because we do have limited time with you, and we want to try to cover all the topics. So just listen to the questions and just keep your answers focused on the questions.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: I apologise to the Trial Chamber. But these are things that really touched me deep down inside, the entire war and everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And I think the Trial Chamber certainly appreciates that, and I apologise for trying to cut you off. It's just because we have limited time. You mentioned that these announcements that your family heard over the radio were calling for people to come to Visegrad. What ethnicity were they trying to attract to Visegrad? What ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: Exclusively Serbs. They were saying that Visegrad had been ethnically cleansed of Bosniaks or Muslims they were called at the time and that we could can get their houses. So that many people from the Neretva Valley went there. But not only they; also people from Sarajevo, or Zenica, or Travnik. Over 20.000 people came to Visegrad from all over. And, of course, accommodation had to be found for all of them, and they had to be fed. It required organisation, and they were also drafted into the army. Many left for Serbia later. They expected the fall of Gorazde. There were announcements to that effect. The Serbs from Gorazde were also expected to come to Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: By the time you arrived Visegrad at the end of August, 1992, how many non-Serbs remained in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: Apart from mixed marriages who weren't bothered by anybody, expect for some minor incidents, the remaining population was locked up in the Uzamnica barracks which was held by the army. There was a unit established to guard them and feed them. They also had work obligation, but there was no other population in the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What happened -- what happened to the houses that the non-Serbs had left behind?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: Most of the houses were not set on fire because they were expected to be given to refugees as accommodation. Then state-owned companies had distributed apartments. They belonged to the companies. So the employees of Varda should go to the apartments owned by Varda, et cetera. Refugees were only given houses. Local population who had relatives there and connections got apartments down-town on the other side of the Drina, that is, the side towards Serbia. Whereas we were sent to the Crnca neighbourhood, as far as possible away from the -- from down-town. So that we refugees would be some sort of a buffer zone between the town itself and the Muslims who sometimes made raids into the town and came as close as a couple of hundred metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: How were the non-Serb houses assigned to Serbs coming to Visegrad? Was there a commission set up, or how was this process conducted?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: A commission was established, and they went from house to house. And depending on the head count, they assigned housing. They were promising that the Muslims would never return so the house would -- could be kept permanently by the people who moved in, but that was a common story at the time in Bosnia and Herzegovina, although it was clear that a house can only be assigned for temporary use. So I got a house at Crnca, but I wasn't allowed to sleep there. I only slept with my father-in-law. On the next day, when I returned home, I found the house robbed, without any furniture, even the firewood was gone. And I -- I inquired who had done it. And I -- they told me, A man Lakic did. And I was angry, and I went about the neighbourhood to see whether I could find a stove somewhere that I could use. And then I saw a couple of soldiers; I thought they were Serbs; and I asked, Do you know a guy Lakic? He robbed me. And he said, Yeah, Lakic would do that. But where are you from? We're from Zenica. But how do you know Lakic? Never mind, sir. You come to our house, we'll give you furniture. And we transported a stove and some things to my house. And only then did I understand that they were actually Bosniaks who lived there. They were killing some people, but they were obviously in no mood to kill me and my brother-in-law, because they obviously recognised us as refugees, like them, and we were up the creek like they were. And --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We didn't understand the witness's last sentence. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you just repeat your last sentence. And then we have to break for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: He said that he had given me his stove. That was his stove, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And I apologise, I'm on the wrong schedule. I guess we're not ready for break.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Okay. You've already mentioned that essentially by the time you arrived in Visegrad, the non-Serbs had left Visegrad. But before arriving Visegrad, did you hear from anyone what had happened to the non-Serbs in that municipality?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: While I was still in Bileca, I spoke to Kospic, an officer of the JNA; he was a Croat. There was also Zajec [phoen], a Slovenian. And I told them that I couldn't get a job in Bileca, although they needed military courts; but because of the relations between Grubac and -- or, rather, the attitude that Grubac and Milicic [phoen] had toward my family in Bilica, because he said to me, Why have you come to Bilica? There is no -- no place here. That is what Papic said to me; he studied with me in Sarajevo. There's no work here. And then I decided to go. Pistols were even drawn for the apartment of Seyad Djogevic [phoen]. And I said, We'd better get out of the way and go elsewhere. And relatives were willing to put us up; it was a relative of my wife's - he was a war orphan from the Second World War, and he had come to Visegrad - who had married another man by the name of Zurovac, and he was looking for an apartment for me. And when he saw that on the other bank it wasn't possible, I looked for an apartment in town -- or, rather, down-town in the vicinity of the prosecutor's office, an apartment of any kind. And I saw there was a house that was partly burnt in Pionirska Street, but the facade was good. Only one room had burned down. But they were saying, No, this is not good enough for you. Let's go to another place. And we found an older house which was damaged, but it could be -- it could be renovated. And I said, Why is this better? This one is better because nobody was killed here. You don't want to live in a house where people were killed and live among their ghosts and have people on your conscience. And that's why --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Sir, would be so good as to speak slowly because everything you said has to be interpreted by the interpreters, but they cannot follow you when you speak so fast.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And, Mr. Drasko, just keep an eye on me because I will indicate to you if you're going too fast or if you need to break for the interpreters. I want to break down what you just told us. You had a conversation about a house that was burnt down on Pionirska Street; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Could you repeat your answer? I don't think it was heard.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: Yes. That house was right across the street in Pionirska. For a long time nobody lived there. Now I see it's been repaired. And I found a big dog there, a tornjak by the name of Lindo, and I took a puppy and the puppy's now with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Just focus on my questions. Who did you have this conversation about this house on Pionirska Street with, and when did you have that conversation?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: When I was looking for apartments on the left bank, there were problems everywhere with breaking and robbing. Then I went to the right bank, but then attacks on that bank started, attacks on Terpentin and on the graveyard, attacks by the Muslim forces. And for the sake of safety, I decided to go to the other bank. And I asked Momo to find something for me, and he found this. And I said, I passed by the command, there's a good house; there's only -- slightly damaged by fire. And he said, No, no, no; don't go there. And never explained to me but I understood that somebody had come to harm there. And he said, Take this house; it belonged to Mustafa Hasim. Nobody was killed here. His wife and he went to Denmark. They are honest people, and you can live there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And this occurred -- was this early September 1992?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: Yes, that's when I was looking for an apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And this individual you had this conversation with, was this a relative of yours?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: Yes, he was a relative. A relative of my wife's.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And did he mention to you that non-Serbs had been killed in a fire in that house?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: No, he didn't. This doesn't seem to be the house where there was a fire, but it had burnt. And somebody may have burned in the house. He never mentioned any details. But he wanted to save my soul. And he told me where I could live normally.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: Unburdened by the souls of the deceased. I do have religious beliefs, and I became more religious in the war. And because of everything that happened to me, I think that gold is bad, that you mustn't take what belongs to another, and if you go to somebody's house you must be grateful and try to do as little damage as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, just to confirm: Are you all right, and are you -- can you go on for another couple of minutes before we have the break, or do you need to take the break now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. All right. I can go on. No problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Before you left for Visegrad, while you were still in Bileca, did you have any conversations with military officials about crimes that were occurring in Visegrad against the non-Serb population?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: Well, here's what they said to me, especially Josip: Lazar, I don't recommend that you go there; crimes were committed there. The Bosniaks were cleansed away. And I said, Where should I go? I'm from the Neretva valley and here there are thousands of problems. Where should I go? Tell me. What should I do? And they're calling me to come there, and they say they may employ me as a judge and that I wouldn't be a soldier anymore so I would get rid of that. My wife seems to be -- able to find a job at the medical centre. My kids can go to school. And that sounds like a normal life. And I didn't know about Visegrad, where it was, and nor did I know about its history expect from the works of Ivo Andric. I knew only what I had read in the book, and I had an idealised image of Visegrad because that was mandatory reading in secondary school, Ivo Andric. And only once before had I passed through Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You mentioned that you were warned about going to Visegrad. Did you hear about the kinds of crimes that were committed against the non-Serb population in the months before you had arrived there, what kind of crimes were committed?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I only heard the warnings from the two JNA officers, but they didn't know any details either.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Were any armed Serb volunteer groups operating in Visegrad between September through December 1992?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: They had various names. The corps was strong -- or, rather, not the corps but the Visegrad Brigade. And it wanted to grow stronger. And they wanted to diminish the reputation of those groups. They wanted cooperation with the Municipal Assembly and the authorities and to prevent lawlessness, especially on the part of those groups. But they were -- there were groups coming in all the time. Some were called locusts. Somebody said that they are some gypsies from Belgrade. Sorry, I don't want to hurt anybody's feelings, but that's what they were called. I know that they roamed the area, but they left very fast, in ten or 15 days. Another group was called Garavi, but they were locals. They were called that because they were smear their faces black before going into action. I know that the -- that Seselj's Men had been released from prison. They were called Seselj's Men; they were locked up for various criminal offences, and they were sent to Bosnia to make havoc there. They didn't even fight; they only stole and raped. I even had a criminal report because they had raped a girl. I didn't know which other units there were. There were also the Russians. A guy had brought a unit that had been in Afghanistan. They only wanted to fight Muslims. They said they wouldn't fight Croats. They prayed to God, some of them drank a bit. There was a Cossack who was killed. There was a doctor who got killed. Valery Pikov [phoen] was an engineer, and he had reserves about Russian soldiers and volunteers. He had an apartment in the state of Russia. He was a civilised man. But very few of them stayed behind -- stayed. They mostly went away fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Were the White Eagles also present in Visegrad when you were there?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: There was rumour about the White Eagles, but I haven't seen anyone -- or, rather, I saw some people, but I don't know whether any one of them was a White Eagle. Because the command was growing stronger, the prosecutor's office was getting off the ground, proceedings were taken against murders, so they didn't have much manoeuvring space, and they were leaving, as the official authorities were getting stronger. So I never even felt the presence of the White Eagles. I never met them. And I had exclusive ties with the command, and I know that they had the best of intentions to introduce law and order into the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, it's 3.40, so I think this is the time for the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If -- can I just ask one question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And then we're done with this topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You mentioned that some of these members of these Serb volunteer groups were former convicts; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: Yes, they were released from prison. And they had also come to the Neretva valley, the same people who were released from prison, to help us once the JNA had withdrawn. And I know back there, on the Neretva, one of these Chetnik commanders pointed his pistol at my head and he said, I understand that you're a reserve officer, Lazar. Take my ten soldiers, but if anyone gets killed, I will kill you. He was a well-known person, but I don't know want to go into that now. He was a personality from political life. And I put away his pistol and said, Don't point your pistol at me. Whoever isn't willing to get killed here can leave right away. Whereas we, who have our homes here, are willing to die here. And we were going to die, but we were tricked. But that group left very soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: And we weren't happy with their presence.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So we have to take our break now, so, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, could I just remind Your Honours, that, if possible, could we have a decision after the next break because we need to make arrangements if the witness is to come on Monday -- I'm sorry, after this break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We haven't forgotten the urgings of the OTP as regards the decision on the motion referred to. It is not -- we are not yet ready; but in the course of today, certainly, we will give our decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Drasko, I want to move to another topic. Can you tell us, Who was the Visegrad basic prosecutor before you?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: Mr. Sahim Muhic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: He was a Muslim. Now he's a Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: I think he left earlier. He left Visegrad earlier. I have all his documentation. Among other things, his award. He came after the war with his son. And when his son got this award, he said, Well, I can see now that my father was a commie, and started laughing. In other words, he was a member of the League of Communists and had an award for that. We kept it for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So between when Mr. Muhic left Visegrad and when you began performing the basic prosecutor work in September of 1992, who was acting as basic prosecutor during that time-period?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: The position was vacated at the time, the premises were empty. Yes, they registered a few cases, but there was no prosecutor there to process them. And then I was invited to work as a prosecutor. They told me I should start working even before I got elected because there were some urgent cases, especially cases involving murder.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: From September 1992, for the rest of that year, was there ever a time when you were unable, as a prosecutor, to receive criminal reports from the police?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: Whatever I received, I had registered. It -- all the criminal reports we received are part of our file of the prosecutor office. Of course, it's the police who chooses what to report and what not. I could not influence them because I was part of the military at the time. I was not at the prosecutor's office all the time, and I could not control what was being taken into the register.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: When you arrived Visegrad at the end of August, was there already a basic court established in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: Yes. Basic court existed. The president of the court was Ms. Milanka Tanaskovic. The judge was another person from Visegrad, a woman who wanted to become prosecutor. And upon my arrival, when I started writing my requests, this women, Rada Bogdanovic, wrote in that my intention was to become a judge because she wanted to be the prosecutor. She added, Well, he can be both prosecutor and a judge. But, in the end, I was appointed the prosecutor and she remained a judge. I took this as some kind of humiliation for us refugees. You're supposed to just sit down and be quiet with your colleagues playing games with you, like she wouldn't know what's the difference between a judge and a prosecutor and why would one be one or the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: These two judges, what were their ethnicities?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: All of them were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: As basic prosecutor, did you become familiar with the members of the police force in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: Yes. There was a police station there, a police station organised. It had a commander, a commissaire. And Josipovic was -- Milan Josipovic was the police commissary. Then they had chiefs of crime investigation department and all the other departments. And they also had the reserve force. They were under their control.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Who was Risto Perisic?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: Risto Perisic was a teacher. He taught literature. And in the wartime period he was appointed as the chief of police. But he was a teacher of Croatian, by profession.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: A Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's take a look at 65 ter 2812.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What we're looking at is the SJB Visegrad salary payment list of employees in October 1992. Mr. Drasko, can you confirm whether this is a list of active SJB Visegrad employees around the time that you were in Visegrad, in 1992?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: Yes, I'm certain about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we look at number 13, we see the name Sredoje Lukic. And there's a remark near his name, that he was --

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: -- that he was suspended on 19 August 1992. Do you know the reasons for his suspension?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: Based on the documentation I read, I know that he released from prison a certain Svjetlana Pavlovic. I didn't know -- I didn't know, at least at the time, who that person was. That this was done without any authorisation. Also, he failed to appear at his work, especially when then there was something to be done. And after the procedure was carried through, he was suspended from the police. That's what I saw in the documents. And we can also see that Milutin Cedo is mentioned here; he committed suicide. He blew himself up using a hand-grenade after a quarrel with his wife. Milan Josipovic also got killed later on. He was killed in his shop.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May this document be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1480, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You mentioned that there was a reserve police force in Visegrad. Can you tell us approximately how many reserve police officers there were in September of 1992?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: I believe that approximately they had -- they were of equal numbers as the regular police, because the area they covered was rather large, and they participated in the fighting as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: By the time you arrived Visegrad at the end of August 1992, were there any non-Serb members of the police in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: No, all of them were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: From September 1992 through the end of the year, did you attend any meetings with the police leadership in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: Yes. I made avail of the opportunity that as the coordinator of the work of state authorities I could organise meetings with judges, police, military administration. We did -- held a few meetings where we analysed our work and discussed ways of improving it. I remember well that, in a way, I complained to some leaders about civilians being physically abused and beaten instead of treated differently, because such cases existed. We mentioned cases of two people who one got mad and the other one committed suicide. And then another man who was beaten by the police jumped out of the window, killing himself. Because these people were afraid and because of this fear, something happened to their personality. They got deranged. And using these examples, I used them to explain that people must not be beaten. And then Josipovic said, No, No, only we can beat. And another man said, No, one must stick to the law. They were rather strict. I didn't bring my car over from Capljina, and I couldn't have registered it in Visegrad. I wasn't allowed to do that with my car. Only when I got back to Capljina I managed to do that. And, on the other hand, policemen who had forged their diplomas would sit into their cars and take me to Ruda. This person's name was Rakil [phoen], and it turned out later that he has provided a counterfeit diploma, and he worked as a policeman using that. And me, as a judge and a prosecutor, I couldn't explain to anyone that I have a driving licence for ten years or more. Even my complaints sent to higher authorities didn't help. I was certainly not privileged. I was all the time in conflicts with them, especially with this man Perisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And that's why I want to address your attention to -- did you attend meetings at which the -- the SJB chief Perisic was present in 1992?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And at those meetings, did you raise these issues of -- of police misconduct with the chief?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: I did not discuss that with them specifically because that's part of their authority. But we did discuss the training of police according to the European Conventions. I gave such proposals to the command and also to -- in relation to the reserve police force and also stressed that they should abide by the legality of the police work. And, on one occasion, I confronted them because there was a refugee who was accused of having stolen some tools, and it turned out that it was something he brought from Zenica. The judge in the -- in his judgement said that the tools should be returned to him, although the man was indicted for theft. And then there was -- there were accusations against us made at the Assembly meeting, but we received support by the Assembly saying, No, you police do your work and let the prosecutors do their work. But we did have problems with him and his friends Savic and Mota Mjilkovic [phoen] precisely because of this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I want to break this down a little bit. You mentioned that police were mistreating persons, they were beating them. What other crimes were the police engaged in, in 1992? Were they engaged in any property crimes, theft, looting?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: I know that there were lootings of property. It was observed on occasions that police officers were involved or present. People complained to me in town. On one occasion, a policeman stopped a religious official's secretary in a hotel in Visegrad and took 600 marks from him, beat him up with a gun, and took even some petrol from his car, and sent him to Sarajevo; but the man, instead of going to Sarajevo, came to me, and then I made a criminal report and processed the case. But the man died in the meantime. He remained in the Federation, namely; and the investigative judge from Visegrad was trying to locate him in Visegrad or somewhere in Republika Srpska. So in the end, this case was never really processed. Again, Novo Rajak had a fist fight with some policemen and then policemen took guns and started shooting him, and then a third man died, brother of Stanko Pecikoza, who was, himself, murdered before then.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let me stop you there before you go too long. These beatings by police officers and these other -- these thefts by police officers, did you bring these crimes to the attention of the SJB chief?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: I wrote a letter, yes. I told him plainly, If you don't know much about law, you should know about literature. And then I quoted Njegos, a poet, who is saying that if the law is in the stick, then --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters apologise, but we cannot do riming.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I sent this letter to him, and I wrote it in this literary style because he wasn't a lawyer and I knew he wouldn't understand the legal writing. But what could I do? I realised that he has no appreciation for the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And when you wrote to Chief Perisic about these police crimes, how did he respond? What was his response to you?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: He was phlegmatic. He normally wouldn't react strongly. He would allow things, he was tolerant. He wasn't attacking peoples. And later on, when Republika Srpska MUP decided to have him dismissed, I know that the chief from Foca, Mr. Mandic, wrote that the man had created Visegrad -- made Visegrad into a crime location and they wanted to dismiss the man. They did dismiss him in the end. But although I was in conflict with him, the municipal authorities asked me to go talk to Karadzic and to ask Karadzic for Perisic to be brought back, although the man was harassing me and took my car. But I went. And we came to Radovan Karadzic's office on the day when the Dayton Agreement was signed. His secretaries told me, He cannot receive you. But then Pecikoza came, who was the director of Terpentin, he came -- I can tell you in brief what this is all about. We want Risto back. And then he said, Go there. And I said, It should be done. So in the end nothing came out of the meeting. The man was not brought back to his position. Instead, he was really dismissed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Just to clarify. Chief Perisic was he dismissed in 1992 or sometime after that?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: It was later, in a later period. At the time of the signing of the Dayton Agreement. I think, maybe if you can remind me, I think it may have been on the 29th of December, 2000 -- no, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... that's fine. That's close enough. When you informed Chief Perisic about these police crimes, did he acknowledge that his police were committing crimes? Did he admit that, yes, they are committing crimes?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: No, he didn't criticise much, and people around him were rather gay. They used to call him Tito, and I asked why. And explained, Well, Tito used to steal but would give to us as well. And this is the same with Risto. So was giving crumbs to the police so that he tolerated them, they tolerated him, and then they protected him as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What were the police doing to investigate and report crimes against non-Serbs in 1992?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: They weren't reporting crimes, especially those against non-Serbs. I never received one single criminal report. And, of course, that's -- you cannot find them in our files, with the exception of minor cattle thefts where farmers would be accused. There was one scandal where chiefs of municipalities forged documents for cars, for instance, Fazlagic Ermin [phoen] comes to Visegrad, a Muslim, and in the middle of the war, a Muslim comes to Visegrad to sell a car. This was obviously a forgery. Srecko Ninkovic was, at the time, chief of the crime department in Rudo, and I received a few criminal reports from him against prominent people and policemen as well. However, this document reached first Milan Josipovic who was supposed to bring them into me, but along the way he showed them to Risto and they simply removed them, they didn't pass them on to the prosecutor's office. I didn't know about them. They didn't reach the files. And when Srecko Ninkovic checked and saw that they weren't in our files, he brought another set of the same criminal reports and only then the proceedings started.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You mentioned Milan Josipovic. What position did he hold with the police in 1992?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: He was a police commander, "komandir."

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, did you ever raise the issue of this failure to investigate crimes against non-Serbs with your superiors, with the higher prosecutor or the republican prosecutor, in 1992?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: I can freely say that I asked for them to come to meetings in Visegrad on several occasions, but they never showed up. Military showed up and police, but these didn't come. And then later on with the war crime commission, me, Simic, and Kostic, when we were supposed to go to Bileca to hand over the documentation I had collected about Dretelj camp and the events there, which remained in Bileca, they sent me back from Pale, Mr. Kladanac and Mr. Staka, telling me, You should deal with thefts in Visegrad; we don't want to know about war crimes; this is a private affair of yours, obviously. It seemed they were criticising. Apparently it was because my wife was in a camp that's the only reason why I wanted to do something about it. So I realised then that nobody's interested in prosecuting war crimes and that the principle of state - it's me - is what applied in our country, and that authorities are not willing to abide by the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's take a look at 65 ter 3419.34.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'm going to ask to you mark a couple of things on this photograph. Mr. Drasko, you already have in your hand the pen. Can you tell us -- we're looking at an aerial photograph. Can you tell us what we're looking at right now?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: This is a photograph of Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you mark with a number 1 on the screen where the SJB building was located in 1992?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: It was across this bridge. This was the building of UPI and this was the police building and here is the building of the recruitment office, the military recruitment office. And this is UPI.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. Can you mark with a number 1, with a numeral 1, on top of the SJB building?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: 1, SJB. This is 2, military recruitment office. And this is UPI.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you mark with a --

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: This is the bridge. And if you go left, will you come to the court and other administrative buildings. And then, across the bridge, if you cross here, there was Borac.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Drasko, please just wait.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Because have you to understand that this is a transcript and therefore you -- what you're commenting on now will not show up in the transcript. So please wait until I ask you a question. Can you mark with a --

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you mark with a -- I guess we're on number 5. Can you mark with number 5 where the prosecutor's office and the court's office was located?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: It's this office, 5. This is 5. This is the building where the court was and the prosecutor's office. And 6 is the municipal building. They were one next to the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You will see directly across the river from the SJB building there is a mosque. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: The mosque should be here on this corner, but it's demolished. You can see that it's demolished. And this is the demolished building. This is where the mosque was.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: That mosque across the river, was it destroyed by the time you arrived in Visegrad in 1992?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: It was totally destroyed. There was just some rubble left. I was fishing here. And here, right across the river, was the Mula Hasic house where I lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: All right. You don't have to mark anymore on the map -- on the photograph. So you --

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Okay. Did you receive any criminal reports or investigation reports regarding the destruction of that mosque from the police?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: No. Neither for one mosque nor the other. I never received any reports concerning them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May this be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1481, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Drasko, you can sit down, if you prefer.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could have on the -- on the screen, 65 ter 1550.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And while we're calling that up, Mr. Drasko, when the police, or anyone for that matter, brought to the prosecutor a criminal report, where was it recorded? Which log-books?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: There were log-books. The main log-book was the KT log-book in which reports against known adult perpetrators of crimes were entered.
