In these log-books, they were ordered by the name or -- of the perpetrator. Whereas, in court, the court log-books, the main element is the number. Then there were also log-books with reports against minor offenders, perpetrators of criminal offences who were minors.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... and was there also --

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: And there are log-books for -- concerning events where on-site investigations are carried out and so on but the crime itself is not yesterday clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I'm sorry, the witness should be instructed to speak slowly because half of his answer was not recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And your -- Mr. Zecevic, your -- what you said was also not recorded. Are you saying that he -- we missed something from his answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, yes. Part of his -- of witness's answer was not recorded because the witness was talking relatively fast. I'm sure the interpreters were unable to catch everything. Because he was listing basically the names of the log-books that were kept in the office of the prosecutor at the time. So if that is important - and I think it is - maybe you should re-address the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes. Let me take you through it, just to save some time. You mentioned there was KT log-book and that was for known adult perpetrators; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And there was also a KTN log-book and that was for unknown perpetrators; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And then I believe you also mentioned there was a KTM log-book and that was for minors?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If you could look at the screen, we see a KT log-book.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Perhaps we could enlarge the B/C/S version a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you confirm, is this the 1992 through 1994 Visegrad Prosecutor's Office KT log-book?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that -- they bound it this way. Now, it didn't look like this formerly. And I can see that now it says, "Republika Srpska District Prosecutor's Office in Eastern Sarajevo;" whereas we were called, "Basic Prosecutor's Offices Visegrad." And -- but prosecutor's offices were restructured. So we are now only one department of the Cantonal Prosecutor's Office -- or, rather, the eastern office in the Republika Srpska. So basic Prosecutor's offices are no longer in existence in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we can turn to page 8 of the B/C/S, page 2 of the English translation. And if we can scroll down a little bit in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Drasko, according to this KT log-book, how many criminal reports were provided to your office in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Maybe we can zoom --

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: In 1992, I think there were only five.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Right. And I think we're looking at them. They're entries number 23, 24, 25, 26, and 27. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we look at the first one, entry number 23, which you received from, according to this log-book, the SJB Visegrad on the 9th of September, 1992, can you tell us --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And perhaps we can zoom in a little bit on that entry.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: -- what was the crime charged?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: It's the criminal offence of endangering the safety of persons. It is a less serious criminal offence, where summary proceedings are possible. And I see that such proceedings, indeed, were launched.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And can you tell us, What was -- were what the ethnicities of the perpetrator and the victim of that crime?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: They were Serbs, all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we look at the second entry, which is number 24, which was received from the SJB Visegrad also on the 9th of September, 1992, can you tell us what was the crime involved in that case?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: It's the criminal offence of murder. Krsto Baranac killed his relative. They were together in the yard; they had been drinking; and he noticed at a point in time that the neighbour's cow was coming to his yard. And he started yelling, Why are you -- why do you leave your cow roaming about? And then he took a log and started beating his neighbour. That neighbour didn't have children. And he beat him up badly with that log which he took from the firewood.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And that's all right. Unfortunately, due to time, let's not go through the facts of the case. I'm just going to ask some very small questions regarding each one. Can you tell us, What were the ethnicities of the perpetrator and the victim?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: They were all Serbs from the same village, Zrnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's look at the third entry, entry number 25, which you received from SJB Visegrad on 2 December 1992. And can you tell us, What was the crime in that case and the ethnicity of the victim and perpetrator?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: Gogic and the injured party Marinko were also neighbours. And there was a quarrel between them. Marinko was a rash plan. Stanimir asked him to return the money that his children had taken from him, and he took a rifle and started chasing him. Later he took a knife, too, and they reached a neighbouring house where there was a rifle in front of the house. And he took that rifle and killed him. So this was qualified as a manslaughter because he -- it wasn't premeditated. And he was also sentenced to a prison sentence. I believe that the -- that the decision came into force too, that there was no appeal.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what was the ethnicity of the perpetrator and the victim?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: They were both Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: The fourth and fifth criminal reports that are recorded in this log-book, entries 26 and 27, they appear to be filed by private citizens. Is that the case?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: Yes. Obred Simsic shot at the window of his neighbour Rosa Simsic because of a quarrel about some land, and she was wounded as a consequence of that. It was qualified as attempted murder because he was aiming at her head, and that's how it was treated.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Both these cases, were they -- were the perpetrators Serbs and the victims Serbs?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: Yes. They were neighbours, Serbs, and this was mostly about property left behind by Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And just to clarify, entry 27 as well, that was a crime committed by a Serb against a -- a Serb?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: In this case, too, Milivoje Droca from Gorazde and Perosi Jakovic from Visegrad, they knew each other well. They were on guard duty in the war, and at a point in time Droca went to the wood because he was taken short, and Pero didn't notice him; he mistook him for an enemy soldier, shot and killed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You had a chance to look at the 1992 entries as well as the 1993 and 1994 entries in this log-book. Were you able to identify any criminal reports of crimes committed by Serb perpetrators against non-Serb victims in 1992?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: No. I reviewed all the log-books and I couldn't find a single case of this type.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And that's consistent with your recollection?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: Yes. There were no reports in that period. But I checked again now to find whether such a report may have been filed any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's look at -- I just want to take a quick look at the 1993 entry.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we can turn to page 10 in the B/C/S and page 4 in English, and I want to look at entry number 4.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this is the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... yes --

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: The persons entered --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. --

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: -- for war crimes committed in the area around Visegrad. There are a number of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... yes, you --

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: Quite a number.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... yes, you -- I think you anticipated my question, but let me ask it. I want to look just right now at entry number 4. And we see that the criminal report charged the perpetrators with a crime under Article 142 of the SFRY Criminal Code and that the crime was committed on the 21st of July, 1992. Are you telling us that that was a war crime charge?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And -- according to this log-book, who submitted the criminal reports? If we can look at the column 4.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: Criminal reports were submitted by the military police and by the civilian police, too. Here, for example, the Visegrad SJB submitted a criminal report, as you can see here, to the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps because they considered them to have jurisdiction. But the corps returned such reports so that they are registered at the prosecutor's office in Visegrad. You can see here the Army of Republika Srpska, the command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, entered as the -- those who submitted the report, but they only returned it, because, actually, the reports had to be submitted to the SJB of Visegrad. Sometimes they were drafted by the command of the Visegrad Brigade, the reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: What is the ethnicity of the perpetrators of this war crime?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: The perpetrators of this war crime were Bosniaks who were then considered -- who are called Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We're not going to look through the following pages in this log-book, but would you agree there are several more criminal reports of war crimes committed by Muslims, submitted by the SJB Visegrad, that are recorded in this book?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: Yes. I reckoned that they were from the area of Rudo and eastern Sarajevo, Serbian Sarajevo, actually, Kopaci, and then some other places: Cajnice Rudo certainly belongs there, and so on. They all, together, submitted about 170 criminal reports. It's all registered. But next to these entries there are the criminal reports themselves -- or, rather, apart from them. They were submitted to the prosecutor's office -- district prosecutor's office at Pale which started functioning and which had jurisdiction for dealing with these reports in accordance with the rules of the ICTY, and forward them for assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: But what happened in 2001, when I went to Trebinje and collected all these reports and submitted them to the prosecutor's office in eastern Sarajevo, then Rajko Bojat bolstered that there was nothing, and he rejected all these criminal reports, and none of them were really dealt with. So whatever was entered here wasn't followed up on. And who knows whether anybody will actually take -- take this up and put -- push it through. There's also the association of former camp inmates who --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: It's all right. Yes, I'm sorry for interrupting you, but we need to focus on 1992. I think you've answered the question that I asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May this be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1481, Your Honours. I apologise. It's -- the number is P1482.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May we have on the screen 65 ter 2971.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We see that we have in front of us a KTN log-book. Can you confirm this is the KTN log-book for the basic prosecutor's office in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 3 of the B/C/S and page 2 of the English. And if we can zoom in on the B/C/S a bit so he can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Drasko, are these the entries in the 1992 KTN log-book?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: Yes. I reviewed it and saw that they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: According to this log-book, how many unknown perpetrator criminal reports were received after you arrived at the prosecutor's office?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: I believe that the information entered here is correct.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We couldn't hear the witness's last sentence because he didn't speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sir, could you repeat your --

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: I -- the information is certainly correct. I checked it. What's entered here is correct. However, I cannot turn pages here.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we can expand out a little bit on the B/C/S version and re-focus it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If I read this correctly, the first three entries were -- predate the conflict; they're from February and March 1992. And it's only the fourth entry that was while you were a prosecutor in 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let me ask it again. If I'm reading this log-book correctly, the first three entries, entries 1, 2, and 3, were from before the conflict, and it's entry number 4 that was entered while you were prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And this number 4 entry, can you tell us, What is the charged crime?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: Yes. It says Snjezana Markovic, Article 143.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Is that a war crime?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: No. I don't think it's Markovic, Snjezana.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: The victim. Is the victim -- what ethnicity is the victim?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: We can see that -- her ethnicity Serbian. She is a Serbian woman.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And we can see she was charged under Article 143 of the SFRY; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: All right. Based upon your review of the entries from 1992 through 1994 in this KTN log-book as well as your personal recollection, were any criminal reports filed for crimes committed in 1992 against non-Serb victims?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: No, they weren't at all. And about Article 143, it should be a war crime. But this is interesting; Markovic, Svjetlana. Svjetlana Markovic may have been a volunteer in the VRS and that's why she was entered here. The 29th of December, 1992. Because Articles 143 and 144 of the Criminal Code of the SFRY, these are the generic offences of the war crime type, from the general chapter -- general section of the Criminal Code. It isn't clear what this is about, but it can be seen in the file itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you. That's all we have for this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May this be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1483, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: The final thing I want to do with you is go over a couple particular crime incidents and find out whether you had any information from the police regarding those crimes in 1992. You already mentioned a house fire on Pionirska Street. Did you receive any information from the police about a house fire that resulted in the deaths of non-Serbs in 1992?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: No, I did not. I didn't receive it from the police, and I didn't know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what about a house fire in Bikavac in 1992 that resulted in the deaths of non-Serbs? Did you receive any information from the police regarding such a crime?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what about the killing of non-Serbs along the banks of the Drina River. Did you ever receive any information from the police regarding such incidents in 1992?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: No. Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... sorry, but this is -- this is so unspecific question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And it has to have territorial limitation because Drina is a long river.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Why would he be informed about the crimes which are not on his territory; that's the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: That's fine. I'll accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: In 1992 - you don't have to go into details - but in 1992, did you know an individual by the name of Milan Lukic?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Did you receive any reports or other information from the police, the SJB Visegrad, about crimes committed by Milan Lukic against non-Serbs in 1992?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What about Sredoje Lukic? Did you receive any information from the police about crimes he committed against the non-Serb population?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: No. Only I found out through private channels about some thefts of his, that he allegedly stole a TV set from a woman. This case was reported.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's look at 65 ter 2860.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Drasko, were you aware that Milan Lukic was arrested at some point in 1992?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And which authorities arrested him? Were they RS authorities, or were they from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: From Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Do you recall roughly when he was arrested?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: I think it was in late 1992 or early 1993 that he was arrested in Serbia for being in possession of arms -- or, rather, he was charged for transporting weapons through Serbia, and then he was charged for possession of weapons, according to their special law.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We're looking right now at a document dated the 2nd of November, 1992. It's an Official Note of an interview with Milan Lukic. It says here that he was arrested on the 26th of October, 1992. Is that consistent with your recollection?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: Yes. I think he may have been arrested at the time -- at that time for the -- the weapons. But mainly because of the weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could turn to the last page of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we look at the second-to-last paragraph, it states that: "Milan Lukic was in custody on the grounds that he was carrying weapons in the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, a misdemeanour under laws of the Republic of Serbia." Is that consistent with your recollection regarding the reasons for his arrest?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: Yes. I don't think that, at the time, he was in detention for Sjeverin and Strpci. It was only for possession of weapons, although in Serbia they knew about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, and if we look at the third paragraph, there's mention that he was interviewed about a murder as well as a kidnapping incident. Can you tell us -- don't give us the name of the person murdered, but was the person murdered -- what was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: A, it is past time for the adjournment; and B, you have exhausted the -- your allotted two hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This is -- if I possibly can do -- one, finish with this document, which won't take, I think, more than another five minutes. And then I would like to show him one more photograph just for him to pin-point places on it just because Your Honours won't be visiting Visegrad during your site visit. So I think, at most, 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: But that will be when we return.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, Madam Korner inquired at the beginning of this hearing if it would make sense to address the issue raised in the Defence motion of 22nd June, responding to the admission of evidence relating to ST-137, and the Chamber has now had a look at it, and we agree that a useful use of the time, Monday and Tuesday when we cannot have Witness 137 come and testify, would be, actually, to re-call ST-179 and -- for the purpose of cross-examining him in light of the information which has come to light in 139's statements and testimony. So we will use Monday and Tuesday for that purpose. And I hope that it will be possible, if you react quickly, to actually call back 179 so as to make sure that he will be here by Monday. But before we go any further, I think I'd like to ask Mr. Zecevic and -- and Mr. Pantelic how much time would you need for the cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, we have a very few specific questions, and we think maximum one hour would be needed for cross-examination of that witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Probably less than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And it be understood clearly that the cross-examination in any circumstance would be limited to the issues that you have raised in your motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Or in your response, paragraph 7, letter (a) to (n), Alpha to November.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honours. It is limited to the -- the cross-examination is limited to the information that we received post festo [sic] from the -- from the delayed disclosure of the witness which was submitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: That is understood. Mr. Pantelic, do you wish to cross-examine?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I don't believe so, Your Honour. We don't have -- maybe, if something just -- just to be sure, to be safe, 15 minutes. But I don't think that we should have any issue for the cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. So, Monday will be reserved for the cross-examination of Witness 179; and the Defence has indicated roughly one hour; and we would give approximately the same time to the Prosecution to re-direct, or re-examine Mr. 179. I hope you will succeed in bringing him here and ask you to take steps immediately to this effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We'll do our best, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Madam Usher, would you bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Welcome back, Mr. Drasko. I'm going to try to wrap up in 15 minutes, so let's try to keep your answers fairly short. We're looking at this document. It's a interview of Milan Lukic by Republic of Serbia authorities. And if we look at the third-to-last paragraph, it mentions this kidnapping incident and mentions that the victims were from a place called Sjeverin. Can you tell us, is that in the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: It's on the border with -- Serbia is along the river of Uvac, and then there are several crossing points, and Sjeverin is immediately on the territory of Republic of Serbia, but then immediately after that they have to enter the territory of Bosnia. So the border -- you can even find a place in Serbia that's an isolated little island within the Bosnian -- an enclave within the Bosnian territory. This is most probably in Serbia, but to reach it you have to go through Bosnia and Herzegovina. But they do have access because it's a road that belongs to both states.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: The victims or the persons who were kidnapped, were they citizens of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: They were all citizens of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: To your knowledge, was Milan Lukic investigated for this kidnapping incident at any point during the conflict, the years 1992 through 1995?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: I know that Sefko Amerovic [phoen] visited to -- visited Rudo and Priboj, also the head of state, the president of the state - what's his name? - Cosic, and they asked for Lukic to be arrested. He was arrested with the assistance of the VRS, and then he was escorted to the Uzice prison. But, later on, VRS commander Pandurovic was later on attacked by people for assisting the arrest -- or, rather, providing information as to where Lukic was. Later on, Caruga - I think his real name is Dragicevic - was saying that he should kill this officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. I want to talk about this kidnapping incident that is reported or discussed in this particular document we're looking in here. Was this incident investigated and was Milan Lukic charged with in kidnapping incident any time during the conflict in BiH, or was it after the conflict in BiH that he was investigated and charged with it?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: I think it was --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I believe my learned friend needs to -- needs to limit his question by saying "by whom." Whether it's the authorities of Serbia, or authorities of Republika Srpska, or some other authorities. For the clarification. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Then I will clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: By anyone, by the Republika Srpska or the Republic of Serbia, did anyone investigate and then charge Milan Lukic with this kidnapping incident during the conflict, meaning 1992 through 1995, or was it only after the conflict?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: Milan Lukic was immediately processed, but it was a farce because he was not charged with kidnapping, he was charged with possession of arms. There was a trial against him in Uzice but only for that crime, not for the kidnapping in Sjeverin or for another case, the case of Strpci.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, in this -- on this occasion where he was detained on these illegal weapons allegations, how long was he held by the law enforcement in the Republic of Serbia? For how long?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: About ten days, I think, he was held. And under pressure excerpted by Milan's people, his mother and father, who came to Perisic, to Visegrad to the police, they asked him back, threatened with rebellion, and they wanted him to be released.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: After 1992, was Milan Lukic still in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm really sorry. I note that the part of the answer 63, 14, in relation to Perisic, what mother and father of Milan Lukic did to Perisic was not recorded. If the witness can repeat that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Okay. Just returning very briefly to your prior answer, you mentioned that the parents of Milan Lukic went to SJB Chief Perisic, and what did they do?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: They disarmed the police. They lined up the policemen and said, If anything happened to him, we'll have a rebellion. They brought some other special forces with him which threatened with a small war erupting in Visegrad. Everybody was praying to go God that Lukic does not come back to Visegrad, but they asked for his release and for the return of weapons. Even I was sent to go to Serbia. I talked to the police. They did not give me the weapons. They gave the weapons to Zika who was in charge of Visegradska Banja. He got the weapons so that he can brag about it. And then I went to the prosecutor, Slobodan, who gave me books. We had a chat, and I realised it was all just a farce and that they don't want to charge him for the kidnapping. They only tried him for that later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And you said that Milan Lukic was released. Did he return to Visegrad in -- later in 1992 and in 1993? Was he in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: He returned to Visegrad and was, again, arrested, I think, on this second occasion in relation to Strpci. He became a businessman in Visegrad, opened a cafe called Atina. Sredoje also opened a cafe or a bar. They both became businessmen.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May this document be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1484, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, finally, I want to show you 65 ter 3419.33. While we're waiting for this document, Mr. Drasko, you said that Milan Lukic was arrested a second time, on a second occasion. Was this in 1993 or 1994? When was it?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: I think it was in 1993 -- or 4th; I'm not sure. But I know that he was again not charged with kidnapping in Strpci, that he was also, again, released. And at the time he had already this catering facility, Atina, in Visegrad, and he was soon released. He wasn't tried for kidnapping until 2001 or 2002. Serbia then tried him and Dragicevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We're looking in front of us at a -- an aerial photograph. Can you confirm that this is an aerial photograph of the area of Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: Yes. This is a photograph showing, depicting the area of Visegrad, we can see here --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... before you start -- before you comment on it, let's -- let's get -- hold on. Just hold on.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May we scroll over to the -- to the right, yes. All the way, all the way.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: Yes, this is better, so I see the other bridge as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... very good. Now, can you mark, roughly, with a number 1, using the pen, can you mark with a number 1 where the SJB was located in 1992?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: The old bridge ... just let me focus for a moment. This is the old bridge. The old bridge. And this up here is the new bridge. This is Bikavac settlement, the Bikavac settlement.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sir, since you've found the Bikavac settlement, can you mark with a number 1 the Bikavac settlement.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: This -- this is Bikavac. The new buildings there. That's Bikavac.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Okay. Can you put a number --

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: This is the new bridge, the blue bridge. And this here is the old bridge. And this bridge here is at the entrance into the city centre. Next to that bridge is the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sir, yes, but we need you to be quite organised with this so that we can get this into evidence. Can you mark, with a number 1, Bikavac. With a number 1.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: This is number 1, Bikavac.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... now with a --

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: I don't know whether you see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We see it, and it looks kind of like two triangles, but we will accept in the record that that's a number 1. Can you mark with a number 2 where the SJB building was located?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: It doesn't leave mark at the same place where I draw it. It it's a bit to the right from where I want it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Why don't we clear it and try it one more time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sir, if you can just hold on. I think what we're going to do is --

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: It is off the mark about 30 centimetres to the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can we clear the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And then what we'll do -- Mr. Drasko, just follow my instructions exactly so we make sure that the exhibit is properly marked. If you can please now mark with a number 1 - just a line - where Bikavac settlement is.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, can you -- you showed us before that the SJB building was near the water edge and near a bridge. Can you mark with a number 2 where that SJB building is on this aerial photograph.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: Yes, it's off to the right again. Maybe 10 to 20 centimetres.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Okay. Could you mark the number 2.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: This pen is off to the right. It's impossible. The pen is not precise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: May I suggest we use a physical photocopy of the picture, if have you it. Because apparently the electronic system is not calibrated at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, for the suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Drasko, what I'm going to do is I'm going to hand you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: -- this exhibit, 65 ter 3419.33, and ask you to mark with a regular pen these few locations.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: The old bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So mark, with the number 1, Bikavac.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: Police station, 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And then can you mark with a number 3 where Pionirska Street is located.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And, finally, can you tell us, What's the distance between the SJB and Pionirska Street roughly, in metres?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: 400 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May this be admitted into evidence. Or do we have to publish it first? I --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Drasko, that's fine. We're just going to publish it for the Trial Chamber and for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: It's admitted and marked as an exhibit. But, technically speaking, I'm not sure what is -- what has been tendered, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, obviously we had to go through the old fashioned way of a manual photograph, and the witness has marked on it three locations: 1, Bikavac; 2, the SJB building; and, 3, Pionirska Street.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit P1485, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can -- can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I can see 1 and 2 on the map -- ah, 3 is up there. Right. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a long street. It's all the way up there. It starts at Cadjava Kafana, it's a one-way street, and leads towards Banpolje. It's a very long street.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, that completes my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Before counsel for the Defence commences the cross-examination, I have been alerted, Mr. Olmsted, to the fact that the OTP requests three minutes. My experience is that such precise estimates of time tend to cause problems particularly at the end of the day sittings. Should I alert counsel to five minutes that you would need, rather than three?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sure, let's round it up to five.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thanks. [Microphone not activated] Mr. Cvijetic, counsel for the Prosecution has requested five minutes to deal with housekeeping matters, so would time yourself accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation], Mr. Drasko, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I'm Slobodan Cvijetic, attorney-at-law, and one of the Defence counsel on the Defence team of the accused, Mr. Mico Stanisic. I will now try to elicit some more precise information from you concerning the sequence of events that led to your appointment as public prosecutor in Visegrad. As far as I understood, you were officially appointed on 31st of October, 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: However, there's something that caught my attention, and I noticed it in your statement, too. After that, you were also in the army as member of the so-called TG Rudo, tactical group?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: TG Rudo, yes, Visegrad Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I deliberately spelled it out for the Bench to know what TG stands for, and I said that it is actually a tactical group. As member of that tactical group, you carried out some military missions; correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: [No verbal response]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I don't believe that your answer was recorded. You must give an oral answer.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So practically, from the 31st of October on, you acted as prosecutor only temporarily because, parallel to that, you also had duties in the military; correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: [No verbal response]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Now please give an oral answer because it wasn't recorded. Is what I say correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: It is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: If I remember well, you said that you were practically requested or asked to deal with some demanding and urgent cases, mostly murders, for the perpetrators to be brought to justice; correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me when I say, then, won't you, that there was no organised and systematic activity of the prosecutor's office before 1993; correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: In 1993, you mentioned a date. Let us just check its significance. I believe you said that you stayed a member of the TG Rudo until the 31st of January, 1993; correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Can we then conclude that only after that date did you start working as a prosecutor in an organised fashion?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Furthermore, I noticed in that KT log-book, when Mr. Olmsted showed it to you, a large gap in the entries, starting from March 1993 [as interpreted] through, I believe, August or September of the same year; correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Furthermore --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, it has been recorded wrongly. The year in question is 1992, not 1993, as recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: After that, in 1992, only the urgent cases that you were asked to take over were entered in the log-book.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the second sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Please repeat the second sentence.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: The court registry entered it in the log-books.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. This was going to be my next question, basically. As far as I could tell from your statement and from what you said, you only got a registry clerk in 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The speakers overlapped. The answer has to be repeated. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Do repeat your answer now.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: Jela Rosic was hired as a clerk then. She started working permanently at the prosecutor's office then. She was under a work obligation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Drasko, there's something I should have pointed out before Mr. Cvijetic began his cross-examination. Inasmuch as the two of you speak the same language, you have to bear in mind, both of you, that time has to be allowed for the interpretation of question and the answer so that it is properly recorded in the transcript. So that the -- be aware of that gap between the question and when you begin your answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So we can say that the small prosecution team was only established in 1993. And when I say that, I mean auxiliary personnel, too. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please see Exhibit 1D03-4295.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I suppose that you recognise the decision on your appointment as public prosecutor in Visegrad. Can you see it on your screen?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And it, indeed, reads that on the 31st of October, 1992, you were officially appointed?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that this is a document that the witness is obviously familiar with, and I don't think that it is contested, so I seek to tender this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Is there any issue as to his having been appointed as the public prosecutor? Why do we need the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if we need a document to establish the exact date when the witness was appointed, and there was much discussion about this, I believe that it can harm no one to have a document about his appointment. But I don't insist on its being tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I didn't appreciate that the date of his appointment was an issue. The -- Mr. Olmsted?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: No, in fact, I elicited that from him during examination-in-chief that he was formally appointed on 31st of October. And, as he testified, he -- he began functioning as a prosecutor much earlier than that, in September. So there is no dispute as to when his formal appointment was made.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe that the exact date when the witness started working is more topical now than ever because it concerns the issue of the legality of his activity until that date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D332, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, what is the 65 ter number of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I continue, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Drasko, do you remember who actually made the proposal that you be appointed?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: I was invited by Mr. Branimir Savovic to write an application. I left the command to the basic court because they had typists who could type the application. Radomira Bogdanovic suggested that she write it. But then I noticed that she wrote that I was applying for the position of judge rather than prosecutor. Then I corrected her. And then she wrote that it was an application for both a judge and a prosecutor. She took the opportunity because she had a typewriter, although I can type with ten fingers, and I accepted to run for both positions, because probably she wanted to apply for the position of prosecutor. The two of them were the only ones there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I must stop you here because you haven't answered my question. Who officially submitted the proposal to the Ministry of Justice or to the Assembly of the RS for you to be appointed?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: I don't know who did it officially, but I handed my application to Branimir Savovic at his office.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Then you must tell us who Mr. Branimir Savovic is.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: Branimir Savovic, at the time, was the president of the municipality of Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we please see document 1D03-4292. Your Honours, this document was sent to the translation service, but I'm not sure that we've received a translation yet. I'll -- I would ask this document to be enlarged for the witness to be able to see it better.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Drasko, I can see from this document that the proposal for your appointment was submitted by the Wartime Commission of the Visegrad Municipality. Can you see it?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And I'm sure you will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Cvijetic, what is this document? We have no idea what we're looking at now.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I am trying to provide you the basics through the witness before we submit, of course, the translation. This is a proposal regarding appointment, Mr. Lazar Drasko, to the position of public prosecutor. We in the Defence find it relevant because of who submitted the proposal. Based on this document, based on the heading, we can see that it was the Wartime Commission of the Serbian Municipality of Visegrad. And my question to the witness was whether he could confirm that it was the Wartime Commissioner Office that sent this document to the Ministry of Justice and Administration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And why -- sorry. And why is that relevant?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it will be clear once I've shown to the witness the documents related to the appointment of the entire police station and based on whose request. I'm trying to demonstrate the role of the local authorities in appointment of justice and police organs in Visegrad. We will just need to see the last page of this document and the signature there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And that will be all that I will be showing to you now. Can you confirm this was signed by Branimir Savovic?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: [No verbal response]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: It should state "Branimir Savovic." Can you repeat your answer, please?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: Yes, Branimir Savovic. But it is clear that this is not my text, that they used my text as the basis for this, my application. Because the application does not contain my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: There's just one note in bold writing. It says: "Dispatch received via radio station." Can you comment on this, please?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know how they worked at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: My question related to this document is the following: Have you seen this proposal ever before?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: No. I only know about my application, the one I submitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, although the witness has not seen this proposal, I believe that it should go together with the decision on his appointment, which is already in the evidence. The witness confirmed that he was proposed to this position, to be appointed to this position, by Mr. Savovic. And to have a clear picture about how he was appointed to his position, I would like to ask for this document to be marked for identification until we have a translation of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, we don't, of course, object to it being marked for identification. But as far as it being admitted down the road, well, we need a translation, 1; and, 2, as my learned friend pointed out, this witness knows nothing about this document. I can't see how this witness is the -- can tender it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, the -- there are two issues here. One is that, as counsel on both sides have indicated, the well-worn path that we have set out for documents of this nature is that if, in the Chamber's view, they are potentially admissible - let me put it that way - that they're marked for identification pending the translation. But the second issue is that the most that I -- the highest that this document can be taken, if I under Mr. Cvijetic correctly, is that it -- its relevance is only its marriage to the document that was last reluctantly admitted. So what -- how does this assist? Because the document that was -- that's still up on the screen in English was - as counsel would recall - admitted after some disputation, and the -- in the Chamber's view, it was of tangential relevance only. So I don't know how we are going to be assisted by a document which, as I said, at its highest, is only married to that tangential document. Put it simply, do we need this even after it's translated?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe the full answer to this, we will have only after I've -- I've shown the next document, the document that deals with how the public security station of Visegrad was established. And only then maybe one can reach an informed decision about usefulness of this document. Let me just remind you, with all due respect, Your Honours, that you admitted several military reports that the witness did not know, was not familiar with, yet he confirmed the contents. So what I'm doing here is I'm abiding by that approach. And I do believe that this document is of higher quality than the military reports that were admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Except, Mr. Cvijetic, that this line of documents relates exclusively to his appointment, the fact of which is not in dispute. Anyway, you have another document in train which would show us how this is relevant. Perhaps you can move on to that and then renew your application in respect of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Your Honours. I'm afraid I won't have time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Cvijetic, I -- Mr. Cvijetic, I have one other matter to raise. You said to -- in order to get this document marked for identification, you said that the witness confirmed that he was proposed to this position by Mr. Savovic. I don't think he did so. You asked him to assist you with an untranslated document, and he's confirmed that the document was signed by this gentleman but he doesn't know anything about it, so he can't confirm that he -- he was appointed by this gentleman. He can confirm that this document is signed by this gentleman. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, maybe you haven't heard the witness who, at page 74, stated that he handed over his application for this appointment to the said Mr. Savovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Am I right, Mr. Drasko? You can answer now.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: There is no contention about the fact that I was appointed by the Assembly of Republika Srpska. It is also clear that I submitted an application for the position of the public prosecutor -- of the prosecutor. My colleague also added in that I applied for the position of the judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Whom did you hand this document to?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: I took it to the municipality and handed it to Mr. Savovic. You cannot see my signature here. They must have formed a file, but my application must be part of it, somewhere in the ministry, because they must have sent my application to Sarajevo as well. My application must be there, including my signature, because I agreed to be a -- positioned -- to be put to that position.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So you confirm that the Wartime Commission and Mr. Savovic worked further on your application and then forwarded it; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR DRASKO
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Well, is -- does the witness know that he was proposed to the Assembly by this Mr. Savovic? He said -- he said he handed over his application to this gentleman, but that doesn't mean that he was proposed to the Assembly by this gentleman or by the War Committee. If he knows that, that's okay. Let the record show it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat his answer, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... so you know that that was the case, that you were proposed by the War Committee?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I submitted an application, and then it's upon them to choose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Hank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the essence of my proposal was to confirm this case of mine by putting this into evidence; but, of course, I'm -- for the time being, proposing only for it to be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, that's not entirely correct, unless I've misunderstood you. You told us that the relevance of the appointment of this witness as prosecutor in Visegrad was to show the larger image about not only who appointed or decided who should be appointed as prosecutor but also who decided to be appointed as members of the police. That last part we haven't heard anything about. So if this is your point, then get on with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I see the time, but the document that will help us with this second issue is the following document. It's a broader document. I will have some other questions to put to the witness in relation to these other topics, but I don't think we have time for that at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. So we would resume this issue tomorrow morning. Mr. Drasko, the trial is about to adjourn for the day. We aren't going to rise immediately. The usher will escort you from the courtroom before we rise. But before you leave, I am obliged to remind you that, having been sworn as a witness, you can not have any communication with the lawyers from either side, nor in your discussions outside the courtroom can you speak about your testimony. So we resume in this courtroom tomorrow morning at 9.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, first I have just a notification: This is to inform the court that we uploaded an official translation for P510, which has the ERN ET -- P0035093. And the issue I wanted to raise with -- oh, there's more. P0035108. As well as an official translation of P530 with the ERN 0018-4319, 0018-4333-ET. Thank you. That was the message. Now, I just want to notify the Trial Chamber that, as far as ST-179 is concerned, we have contacted him, and he is available to come. The bad news, which may not be bad news, is that typically it takes five working days to get a visa for him. But they're going to try to expedite it. We have a witness who's scheduled to testify to start Wednesday, and that witness cannot be moved up at all because it's -- the arrangements have already been made. So, at worst case scenario, ST-179 would start on Tuesday. But hopefully he will be here on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Olmsted. So we take the adjourn -- Sorry, Mr. Zecevic, you were about to say something?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, I was expecting you would say that we were adjourn, so I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we take the adjournment to 9.00 tomorrow morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 29th day of June, 2010, at 9.00 a.m. 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.59 p.m.,
